edges.title: Debussy and the Javanese gamelan, Paris, 1889

works.from: Javanese gamelan at the Exposition Universelle, Paris (1889)

edges.claim: At the Paris Exposition of 1889, [[debussy]] heard a Javanese gamelan. Features of it appear in the piano piece Pagodes, which has a gong-like bass beneath a pentatonic tune, with faster notes above. He later wrote that Javanese music “obeys laws of counterpoint which make Palestrina seem like child’s play”.

sources.title: Brent Hugh: Claude Debussy and the Javanese Gamelan

edges.title: Debussy’s Prélude à l’après-midi d’un faune after Mallarmé

works.from: L’après-midi d’un faune (poem, 1876)

edges.claim: [[debussy]] called his prelude “a very free illustration” of Mallarmé’s poem. Gustave Doret conducted the première in Paris on 22 December 1894, with Mallarmé in the audience. Afterwards the poet wrote to Debussy that the music went further than his text, “into nostalgia and into light”.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Prélude à l’après-midi d’un faune

edges.title: Hokusai’s Great Wave on La Mer’s cover

works.from: The Great Wave off Kanagawa (c. 1830–32)
works.to: La Mer, first edition of the orchestral score (Durand, 1905)

edges.claim: Durand put Hokusai’s The Great Wave off Kanagawa on the cover of [[debussy]]’s La Mer in 1905. The cropped image keeps roughly the left half of the print, with the great wave poised above a smaller one.
edges.note: The cover is documented. How far Hokusai’s image shaped the composition remains a matter of interpretation.

sources.title: Eastman School of Music, Sibley Library: Claude Debussy, La Mer

art.file: File:Debussy - La Mer - The great wave of Kanaga from Hokusai.jpg
art.caption: Cover of the first edition of Debussy’s La Mer (Durand, 1905), with a detail of Hokusai’s The Great Wave off Kanagawa.

edges.title: Tristan in Debussy’s Golliwogg’s Cakewalk

works.from: Tristan und Isolde, Prelude (1859)

edges.claim: In Golliwogg’s Cakewalk, Debussy alludes satirically to [[wagner]]’s Tristan und Isolde. The opening bars turn the Tristan chord into a syncopated arpeggio, and the middle section is interrupted several times by a Tristan phrase marked avec une grande émotion. Debussy had heard the first act of Tristan at the Concerts Lamoureux in 1887 and judged it “decidedly the finest thing I know”.

edges.title: Debussy’s orchestration of Satie’s Gymnopédies

works.from: Debussy’s orchestration of Gymnopédies Nos. 3 and 1 (1897)

edges.claim: In February 1897, when Satie’s popularity was waning and his finances were deteriorating, [[debussy]] orchestrated the third and first Gymnopédies to draw public attention to his friend’s music. When Debussy published the scores two years later he reversed the numbering, so that Satie’s first became his third. The two had met in 1890 and shared an experimental approach to composition.

edges.title: Satie’s Sonneries de la Rose+Croix for Péladan

works.from: Salon de la Rose+Croix, Paris (10 March–10 April 1892)

edges.claim: Sâr Joséphin Péladan invited [[satie]] to become official composer to his Ordre de la Rose-Croix Catholique. At its first Salon, from 10 March to 10 April 1892, Satie’s three fanfares for harp and trumpet were played before the Solemn Mass of the Holy Ghost. They were published as Sonneries de la Rose+Croix.

sources.title: Interlude: Erik Satie, The Rosicrucian Adventure

edges.title: Strauss’s Also sprach Zarathustra after Nietzsche

works.from: Also sprach Zarathustra (1883–85)

edges.claim: [[richard-strauss]] conducted the first performance of his tone poem in Frankfurt on 27 November 1896, and named its sections after chapters of Nietzsche’s book (“Of the Backworldsmen”, “Of the Great Longing”). Strauss said that he had not meant to write philosophical music or to portray Nietzsche’s work. He had intended “to convey in music an idea of the evolution of the human race” up to Nietzsche’s idea of the Übermensch.

sources.title: Rhode Island Philharmonic: The story behind Strauss’s Also sprach Zarathustra
Indianapolis Symphony Orchestra: program notes, Also sprach Zarathustra

edges.title: Beethoven’s funeral march in Strauss’s Metamorphosen

works.from: Symphony No. 3, “Eroica”, Marcia funebre (1804)

edges.claim: At the end of Metamorphosen, [[richard-strauss]] quoted the first four bars of the Marcia funebre from [[beethoven]]’s “Eroica” Symphony and wrote beneath them “IN MEMORIAM!”. A direct quotation from bar 3 of the march also appears earlier in the score as one of the work’s themes.

edges.title: Sibelius and Larin Paraske, Porvoo, 1891

works.from: Larin Paraske’s rune singing, Porvoo (1891)

edges.claim: At the end of 1891 [[sibelius]] travelled with the aesthetician Yrjö Hirn to Porvoo to hear the Izhorian rune singer Larin Paraske. Sibelius recalled that he mainly noticed how a rune singer uses Finnish, prolonging and stressing the last syllables of words, and that he did not yet realise how famous she was. Kullervo, whose vocal movements set runos of the Kalevala, followed in 1892.
edges.note: Hirn’s recollection and Sibelius’s own account place a hearing at Porvoo at the end of 1891, while Sibelius later claimed he first met Paraske on his 1892 honeymoon in Lieksa. That he heard her is documented. Where and when he first did so is not settled, and the extent to which her singing shaped Kullervo is a matter of interpretation.

sources.title: Finnish Music Quarterly: “Utterly Finnish, peculiarly original”
sources.locator: Hirn’s account of the 1891 Porvoo trip

edges.title: Scriabin’s Preludes, Op. 11, and Chopin’s Op. 28

works.from: Chopin, 24 Preludes, Op. 28 (1839)

edges.claim: [[scriabin]]’s twenty-four Preludes, Op. 11, follow the same circle of fifths as [[chopin]]’s Op. 28. Each major key is paired with its relative minor, and the set covers all twenty-four keys.
edges.note: The sources describe the likeness of construction between the two cycles; no statement by Scriabin that he modelled Op. 11 on Op. 28 was found.

edges.title: Janáček’s Kreutzer Sonata Quartet after Tolstoy

works.from: The Kreutzer Sonata (novella)

edges.claim: [[janacek]] wrote his First String Quartet between 13 and 28 October 1923, after Tolstoy’s novella The Kreutzer Sonata, which took its title from [[beethoven]]’s violin sonata of that name. He had used the novella once before, in a Piano Trio of 1908–09; the trio is lost, and surviving fragments suggest similarities to the quartet. The Czech Quartet gave the first performance in Prague on 17 October 1924.

edges.title: Elgar’s setting of Newman’s Dream of Gerontius

works.from: The Dream of Gerontius (poem, 1865)

edges.claim: [[elgar]] had owned a copy of Newman’s poem since at least 1885, and in 1889 he was given another as a wedding present; that copy carried handwritten transcriptions of notes made by General Gordon. He had considered setting the text for years before he composed it for the Birmingham Triennial Festival, where The Dream of Gerontius was first performed on 3 October 1900.

edges.title: Beethoven’s Pathétique and Elgar’s Nimrod

works.from: Piano Sonata No. 8, “Pathétique”, slow movement (1799)

edges.claim: Elgar said Nimrod came from a day when he was ready to give up composing and his publisher August Jaeger urged him on, pointing to [[beethoven]], who wrote more and more beautiful music despite his worries, and singing the theme of the slow movement of the “Pathétique” sonata. Elgar told Dora Penny that the opening bars of Nimrod were made to suggest that theme: “Only a hint, not a quotation”.

edges.title: Puccini at Aida, Pisa, 1876

works.from: Aida (1871)
works.to: Puccini’s career in the opera house

edges.claim: In 1876, aged eighteen, [[puccini]] walked about twenty kilometres from Lucca to Pisa to hear the first local performance of [[verdi]]’s Aida. He said later that when he heard it in Pisa he felt “a musical window had opened for me”. The experience is credited with turning him from church music to the theatre.

sources.title: Choirs.org.uk: Puccini, Messa di Gloria, programme notes

edges.title: Chinese music-box melodies in Puccini’s Turandot

works.from: Chinese melodies on a music box owned by Baron Fassini-Camossi

edges.claim: Baron Edoardo Fassini-Camossi, a former Italian diplomat in China, gave [[puccini]] a music box that played four Chinese melodies. Puccini used three of them in Turandot, among them the folk melody “Mòlìhuā” (“Jasmine Flower”), which serves as a leitmotif for the princess. In all, eight of the opera’s themes are thought to be based on traditional Chinese music.

edges.title: Schoenberg’s setting of George in the Second Quartet

works.from: Stefan George, Litanei and Entrückung (Der siebente Ring)
works.to: String Quartet No. 2, Op. 10, movements III–IV (1908)

edges.claim: In the last two movements of his Second String Quartet, [[schoenberg]] set poems by Stefan George for soprano, adding a voice to a genre that had never had one. The Rosé Quartet and the soprano Marie Gutheil-Schoder gave the first performance. A critic writing in 1914 called the innovation Beethovenian, a reference to the choral finale of the Ninth Symphony.

edges.title: Schoenberg’s Harmonielehre, dedicated to Mahler

works.from: Gustav Mahler, who died in May 1911

edges.claim: [[schoenberg]] wrote his Harmonielehre in the summer of 1910 and published it in 1911 with the dedication “Dem Andenken Gustav Mahlers ist dieses Buch geweiht” (“This book is dedicated to the memory of Gustav Mahler”). [[mahler]] died on 18 May 1911.

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Arnold Schoenberg and his relation to Gustav Mahler

edges.title: Kandinsky, Schoenberg and the Blaue Reiter, 1911

works.from: Kandinsky’s letters to Schoenberg, from 18 January 1911
works.to: Schoenberg’s contributions to the Blaue Reiter exhibition and almanac (1911–12)

edges.claim: After hearing [[schoenberg]]’s music at a Munich concert on 2 January 1911, Kandinsky wrote to him on 18 January: “In your works, you have realized what I, albeit in uncertain form, have so greatly longed for in music.” Schoenberg visited Kandinsky, Gabriele Münter and Franz Marc in Murnau, and the painters planned an exhibition and an almanac that drew in artists of every medium. The two corresponded until the First World War broke off contact in 1914.

sources.title: Sarah Tanner, thesis on Kandinsky and Schoenberg (Auburn University at Montgomery digital archives)
sources.locator: the concert of 2 January 1911 and the letter of 18 January

edges.title: Kandinsky’s Impression III after Schoenberg’s concert

works.from: Concert of Schoenberg’s music, Munich (2 January 1911)

edges.claim: Kandinsky’s painting Impression III (Concert) was inspired by a concert of [[schoenberg]]’s works in Munich on 2 January 1911, which Kandinsky attended. He wrote to Schoenberg within days, beginning an exchange of letters that lasted until 1914.

sources.title: Sarah Tanner, thesis on Kandinsky and Schoenberg (Auburn University at Montgomery digital archives)

art.file: File:Wassily Kandinsky - Impression III (Concert) - Google Art Project.jpg
art.caption: Kandinsky, Impression III (Concert), 1911, painted after hearing Schoenberg’s music in Munich.

edges.title: Berg’s studies with Schoenberg, 1904–11

works.from: Schoenberg’s teaching in Vienna (1904–11)
works.to: Berg’s early works, from the Piano Sonata, Op. 1

edges.claim: Berg studied counterpoint, music theory and harmony with [[schoenberg]] between 1904 and 1911. He adopted his teacher’s principle of developing variation and, later, the twelve-note technique, which he used in the Lyric Suite and the Violin Concerto.

edges.title: Berg’s Wozzeck after Büchner’s Woyzeck

works.from: Woyzeck (play, 1837)

edges.claim: In May 1914 [[berg]] attended a performance in Vienna of Büchner’s play, left unfinished at the author’s death in 1837, and was moved to set it. The opera that followed, Wozzeck, kept the play’s fragmentary scenes in order and was completed after the First World War.

edges.title: Bach’s chorale in Berg’s Violin Concerto

works.from: Cantata BWV 60, closing chorale “Es ist genug”

edges.claim: Berg wrote his Violin Concerto “to the memory of an angel” after the death of Manon Gropius, and built its last section on the chorale “Es ist genug” from [[bach]]’s cantata O Ewigkeit, du Donnerwort. The last four notes of Berg’s tone row, rising by whole tones, are also the first four notes of the chorale, and in the score a footnote explains the marking CH as the chorale motif. Berg sets the tune a semitone above Bach’s A major, the solo violin giving the first phrase before the clarinets state Bach’s harmonisation.

sources.title: IMSLP: Violin Concerto (Berg), Universal Edition score, 1936

edges.title: Tristan quotation in Berg’s Lyric Suite

works.from: Tristan und Isolde, Prelude (1859)

edges.claim: By Berg’s own analysis, the last movement of [[berg]]’s Lyric Suite develops the Tristan motif along with the rest of its material through strict adherence to the twelve-note series. In January 1977 George Perle was shown a copy of the first printed score annotated in red, blue and green by Berg, which revealed a secret programme about Berg’s love for Hanna Fuchs-Robettin. The suite was publicly dedicated to Zemlinsky, whose Lyric Symphony it also quotes.

sources.title: The Cambridge Companion to Berg: Secret programmes (chapter 8)

edges.title: Webern’s orchestration of Bach’s Ricercar a 6

works.from: Musical Offering, BWV 1079: Ricercar a 6 (1747)

edges.claim: Between December 1934 and early 1935 [[webern]] orchestrated the six-voice ricercar from [[bach]]’s Musical Offering for a chamber orchestra of single winds, harp, timpani and strings. The first performance was in London on 25 April 1935. Webern kept Bach’s notes and divided the lines among the instruments, so that a single melody passes from one instrument to another. He called this principle Klangfarbenmelodie.

sources.title: Universal Edition: Bach/Webern, Fuga (2. Ricercata) a 6 voci

edges.title: Webern’s edition of Isaac’s Choralis Constantinus

works.from: Choralis Constantinus II (early 16th century)
works.to: Webern’s doctoral edition and his later counterpoint

edges.claim: For his musicology doctorate under Guido Adler, [[webern]] edited the second part of Heinrich Isaac’s Choralis Constantinus. In his own compositions he later emulated its “subtle organization in the interplay of parts”.

edges.title: Bartók’s phonograph recordings of peasant songs, 1906–08

works.from: Peasant songs recorded in Békés County and elsewhere (1906–08)
works.to: Bartók’s folk-song collections and the music built on them

edges.claim: [[bartok]]’s first year of substantial folk-song collecting was 1906. That summer he used a phonograph on his first systematic trip, to Békés County, and over the year he collected more than a thousand Hungarian songs and some three hundred Slovak ones. In 1907–08 he went on to Felsőireg and to the Transylvanian regions of Csík and Gyergyó. Following Béla Vikár, he used the phonograph from the beginning to complete his written notes with sound recordings.

sources.title: Institute for Musicology, Budapest: Béla Bartók’s significance in Hungarian folk music research

edges.title: Kodály’s Debussy scores and Bartók, 1907

works.from: Debussy’s scores, brought from Paris by Kodály

edges.claim: From 1907 [[bartok]] came under the influence of [[debussy]], whose compositions his friend Kodály had brought back from Paris. Bartók was by then already collecting peasant music, and French harmony and Hungarian folk material entered his work at the same time.

edges.title: Stravinsky’s studies with Rimsky-Korsakov, to 1908

works.from: Rimsky-Korsakov’s teaching, St Petersburg

edges.claim: While studying law at the University of Saint Petersburg, [[stravinsky]] met [[rimsky-korsakov]] and studied music under him until the older composer’s death in 1908. Soon afterwards Stravinsky met Sergei Diaghilev, who commissioned the ballets for the Ballets Russes that made his name.

edges.title: Lithuanian folk song in The Rite of Spring

works.from: Anthology of Lithuanian folk songs (Warsaw)
works.to: The Rite of Spring, opening bassoon solo (1913)

edges.claim: [[stravinsky]] acknowledged that the opening bassoon melody of The Rite of Spring was derived from an anthology of Lithuanian folk songs, but maintained that this was his only borrowing from such sources. Later scholars have identified several more melodies in Part I that came from the same Lithuanian collection, and Richard Taruskin’s study of the sketches traced further Russian folk sources.

sources.title: The Orchestral Bassoon: Stravinsky, The Rite of Spring
sources.locator: opening solo; notes citing Taruskin, “Russian Folk Melodies in The Rite of Spring” (JAMS, 1980)

edges.title: Stravinsky’s Pulcinella, after music attributed to Pergolesi

works.from: Pieces then attributed to Pergolesi

edges.claim: In Pulcinella, [[stravinsky]] recomposed music that had reached him under Pergolesi’s name for a ballet drawn from commedia dell’arte. It was first danced in Paris in May 1920, with designs by Picasso.
edges.note: The Pergolesi attribution covers music by several composers. The cited account names Domenico Gallo, Unico Wilhelm van Wassenaer, Carlo Ignazio Monza and Alessandro Parisotti among the other possible composers.

edges.title: Stravinsky at Pierrot lunaire, Berlin, 1912

works.from: Pierrot lunaire, Op. 21 (1912)

edges.claim: In the winter of 1912 [[stravinsky]] was in Berlin for performances of his ballets by the Ballets Russes, and attended a performance of [[schoenberg]]’s Pierrot lunaire, conducted by the composer, less than two months after its première. He had already composed the first of his Three Japanese Lyrics as a song with piano, but after hearing Pierrot he decided to score the songs for an instrumental ensemble somewhat similar to Schoenberg’s.

sources.title: Hollywood Bowl: Stravinsky, Three Japanese Lyrics

edges.title: Hymn tunes and town bands in Ives’s music

works.from: Hymn tunes, town-band music, Stephen Foster

edges.claim: The sources of [[ives]]’s tonal imagery included hymn tunes and traditional songs. He also used the melodies of town bands at holiday parades, fiddlers at Saturday-night dances, patriotic songs, sentimental parlour ballads and the tunes of Stephen Foster.

edges.title: Beethoven’s Fifth motif in Ives’s Concord Sonata

works.from: Symphony No. 5, opening motif (1808)

edges.claim: The opening bars of [[beethoven]]’s Fifth Symphony are quoted in each movement of [[ives]]’s Concord Sonata, whose four movements portray Emerson, Hawthorne, the Alcotts and Thoreau. Ives drew on material dating back to 1904, began substantial work around 1909 and largely completed the sonata by 1915; it was first published in 1920.

edges.title: Shostakovich at the Leipzig Bach Competition, 1950

works.from: The Well-Tempered Clavier (1722, 1742)

edges.claim: In 1950 [[shostakovich]] sat on the jury of the first International Johann Sebastian Bach Competition at Leipzig, held for the bicentenary of [[bach]]’s death. The young Tatiana Nikolayeva from Moscow, who had come prepared to play any of the 48 preludes and fugues on request, won the gold medal. Prompted by the competition and her playing, he returned to Moscow and began his own cycle of 24 preludes and fugues, which Nikolayeva premiered in Leningrad on 23 December 1952.

edges.title: Sollertinsky, Shostakovich and Mahler

works.from: Mahler’s symphonies, introduced by Ivan Sollertinsky

edges.claim: [[shostakovich]]’s close friendship with the musicologist and theatre critic Ivan Sollertinsky began in 1927. Shostakovich later said that Sollertinsky “taught [him] to understand and love such great masters as Brahms, Mahler, and Bruckner”. Mahler’s music had a lasting influence on Shostakovich’s style, which combines the grotesque with ambivalent tonality.

edges.title: Shostakovich and Gubaidulina’s Conservatoire examination, 1959

works.from: Shostakovich’s verdict on a Conservatoire examination
works.to: Gubaidulina’s early music at the Moscow Conservatory

edges.claim: [[gubaidulina]]’s music was judged “irresponsible” during her studies at the Moscow Conservatory because it explored alternative tunings. When [[shostakovich]] assessed one of her examinations he encouraged her to continue on her path, although others, among them Tikhon Khrennikov, called it “mistaken”. Her violin concerto Offertorium of 1980 was her breakthrough.

edges.title: Bach’s royal theme in Gubaidulina’s Offertorium

works.from: Musical Offering, BWV 1079: the royal theme (1747)

edges.claim: Offertorium is built on the theme that Frederick the Great gave to [[bach]], the basis of the Musical Offering. [[gubaidulina]] scored the theme in the Klangfarbenmelodie manner associated with Webern, passing it from instrument to instrument so that its colour changes. The piece was her first major breakthrough.

edges.title: Shostakovich’s Fourteenth Symphony, dedicated to Britten

works.from: Symphony No. 14 (1969)

edges.claim: [[shostakovich]] dedicated his Fourteenth Symphony, a song cycle on poems about death, to his close friend [[britten]], who conducted its Western première at the 1970 Aldeburgh Festival.

edges.title: Britten’s Young Person’s Guide on a Purcell theme

works.from: Abdelazer, Rondeau (1695)
works.to: The Young Person’s Guide to the Orchestra, Op. 34 (1945)

edges.claim: [[britten]]’s Young Person’s Guide to the Orchestra, subtitled Variations and Fugue on a Theme of Purcell, is based on the second movement, a rondeau, of Purcell’s Abdelazer suite. It was commissioned for the British educational documentary film Instruments of the Orchestra, released on 29 November 1946.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Young Person's Guide to the Orchestra

edges.title: Auden’s libretto for Britten’s Paul Bunyan

works.from: Libretto for Paul Bunyan (1941)

edges.claim: [[britten]]’s first music drama, the operetta Paul Bunyan (1941), has a libretto by W. H. Auden. The partnership had begun earlier, in the small group of regular contributors to the GPO Film Unit that Britten joined in the 1930s, where Auden was another of the writers.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Benjamin Britten
sources.locator: GPO Film Unit; America and Paul Bunyan

edges.title: Colin McPhee’s Balinese transcriptions and Britten

works.from: McPhee’s piano-duo transcriptions of Balinese gamelan

edges.claim: While in the United States, [[britten]] first encountered Balinese gamelan music through transcriptions for piano duo by the Canadian composer Colin McPhee, who had lived in Bali from 1931 to 1938. The two met in the summer of 1939 and recorded some of the transcriptions together. Britten later used many gamelan elements in the ballet The Prince of the Pagodas, including a simulation of the seven-tone pelog tuning on Western instruments.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Prince of the Pagodas
sources.locator: Influence of Balinese gamelan on the music

edges.title: Poulenc’s Concert champêtre for Landowska

works.from: Wanda Landowska’s Pleyel harpsichord

edges.claim: [[poulenc]] composed his Concert champêtre for the harpsichordist Wanda Landowska, a friend and colleague from 1923. She gave the first performance with the Orchestre Symphonique de Paris under Pierre Monteux at the Salle Pleyel on 3 May 1929.

edges.title: Lili Boulanger’s settings of Francis Jammes

works.from: Poems by Francis Jammes

edges.claim: [[lili-boulanger]]’s song cycle Clairières dans le ciel is set to poems by Francis Jammes. It stands with her three psalms for chorus and orchestra, the diptych D’un soir triste and D’un matin de printemps, and her Prix de Rome cantata Faust et Hélène among the works that made her reputation.

edges.title: Messiaen’s birdsong notations

works.from: Birdsong, notated in the field
works.to: Le merle noir (1952); Réveil des oiseaux (1953)

edges.claim: [[messiaen]] was fascinated by birdsong and notated it around the world. Birds had appeared in several earlier works, but the flute piece Le merle noir was based entirely on the song of the blackbird. The material of the orchestral Réveil des oiseaux (1953) consisted nearly entirely of birdsong heard between midnight and noon in the Jura. From then on he incorporated birdsong transcriptions into his compositions.

edges.title: Messiaen and Debussy’s Pelléas et Mélisande

works.from: Pelléas et Mélisande (1902)

edges.claim: At Nantes, one of Messiaen’s teachers, Jehan de Gibon, gave him a score of [[debussy]]’s opera Pelléas et Mélisande. [[messiaen]] called it “a thunderbolt” and “probably the most decisive influence on me”. He entered the Paris Conservatoire in 1919, aged eleven.

edges.title: Ligeti and Nancarrow’s Player Piano Studies, 1980

works.from: Studies for Player Piano
works.to: Ligeti’s Piano Études and Piano Concerto (1980s)

edges.claim: [[ligeti]] first came across Nancarrow’s name through a Berlin festival of mechanical music in January 1980, when he saw a score page of Study No. 36 in the festival catalogue and was taken with its complexity and temporal layering. He called Nancarrow’s music “the greatest discovery since Webern and Ives”. His Piano Études draw on sources including gamelan, African polyrhythms, Bartók, Monk, Bill Evans and Nancarrow.

sources.title: Nancarrow und Ligeti (nancarrow.de, in German)
sources.locator: the Berlin festival, January 1980; Study No. 36

edges.title: Boulez’s studies with Messiaen, 1944–45

works.from: Messiaen’s private seminars and Conservatoire class

edges.claim: In June 1944 [[boulez]] approached [[messiaen]] and asked to study harmony with him. Messiaen invited him to attend the private seminars he gave to selected students, and in January 1945 Boulez joined his advanced harmony class at the Conservatoire de Paris. He also studied counterpoint privately with Andrée Vaurabourg and, with René Leibowitz, twelve-note technique.

edges.title: Boulez’s “Schoenberg is Dead”, 1952

works.from: Schoenberg’s twelve-note music

edges.claim: A 1952 article in the British journal The Score, published shortly after [[schoenberg]]’s death, first brought [[boulez]] international attention as a writer. In it he attacked Schoenberg for conservatism and set him against the radicalism of Webern. The article caused widespread controversy. Boulez had learned twelve-note technique privately with René Leibowitz, a champion of Schoenberg.

edges.title: Boulez’s Pli selon pli after Mallarmé

works.from: Sonnets by Stéphane Mallarmé
works.to: Pli selon pli, “Portrait de Mallarmé” (first performed 1960)

edges.claim: [[boulez]]’s Pli selon pli (“Fold by fold”), subtitled Portrait de Mallarmé, is a work in five movements for solo soprano and orchestra whose text is drawn from sonnets by Mallarmé. It was first performed in 1960 at Baden-Baden, sixty-six years after [[debussy]] based the Prélude à l’après-midi d’un faune on another Mallarmé poem.

edges.title: Cage and Boulez in Paris, 1949

works.from: Sonatas and Interludes for prepared piano (1946–48)

edges.claim: [[boulez]]’s friendship with [[cage|John Cage]] began in 1949, when Cage was visiting Paris. Cage introduced him to two publishers, Heugel and Amphion, who agreed to take his recent pieces, and Boulez helped arrange a private performance of Cage’s Sonatas and Interludes for prepared piano.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Pierre Boulez
sources.locator: Early career: John Cage and Karlheinz Stockhausen

edges.title: Feldman and Cage after Webern’s Symphony, 1950

works.from: Webern’s Symphony, Op. 21 at Carnegie Hall (January 1950)

edges.claim: In January 1950 [[feldman]] met [[cage|John Cage]] walking out of Carnegie Hall, where both had gone to hear the New York Philharmonic under Dimitri Mitropoulos play Webern’s Symphony, Op. 21. Feldman soon moved into Cage’s apartment building on Grand Street, and through Cage met Jackson Pollock, Philip Guston and Frank O’Hara.

edges.title: Feldman’s Rothko Chapel and Rothko’s paintings

works.from: Mark Rothko’s paintings in the Rothko Chapel, Houston

edges.claim: In the 1970s [[feldman]] wrote a number of pieces about twenty minutes long, among them Rothko Chapel (1971), written for the building in Houston that houses paintings by Mark Rothko. He drew on abstract expressionist painting and knew its painters through [[cage|John Cage]], who introduced him to Jackson Pollock, Philip Guston and Frank O’Hara.

edges.title: Pärt’s chant studies before Für Alina

works.from: Gregorian chant and the Notre Dame School
works.to: Für Alina (1976) and the tintinnabuli style

During that time he joined the Orthodox Church and studied Gregorian chant, the Notre Dame School and classic vocal polyphony. In 1976 he arrived at a new musical language that he called tintinnabuli, first heard in the piano piece Für Alina.

M. Jones’s Studies in African Music on the Ewe, for Drumming (1970–71), which he began composing shortly after his return.

edges.claim: In the summers of 1973 and 1974 [[reich]] studied Balinese gamelan, the semar pegulingan and the gambang, at Seattle and Berkeley. The experience influenced his Music for Mallet Instruments, Voices and Organ (1973); in 1974 he began writing Music for 18 Musicians.

edges.claim: [[kurtag]]’s Kafka-Fragmente, Op. 24 (1985–87), for soprano and violin, sets extracts from Kafka’s journals and letters as forty short pieces in four sections. Kurtág was drawn to the bareness of Kafka’s language, to its sadness and despair, its humour and its depth. The soprano Adrienne Csengery and the violinist András Keller gave the first performance at the Witten Festival of Contemporary Chamber Music in 1987.

edges.claim: In 1993 [[saariaho]] came to know the work of the twelfth-century troubadour Jaufré Rudel, the poet of far-off love (amor de lonh). She had not thought herself capable of writing an opera until she saw Peter Sellars’s staging of Messiaen’s Saint François d’Assise at the 1992 Salzburg Festival. L’Amour de loin (“Love from Afar”), to a libretto by Amin Maalouf, was first performed at the Salzburg Festival on 15 August 2000.

edges.title: Price’s studies with Chadwick, Boston, 1903–06

works.from: Composition with Wallace Goodrich and Frederick Converse; private lessons with George W. Chadwick, director of the conservatory
works.to: Price’s training in Boston, 1903–06, before her Symphony in E minor (1931)

edges.claim: In 1903 Florence Smith, later [[price]], enrolled at the New England Conservatory in Boston. She completed the four-year course in three years and graduated in 1906 with two diplomas, a soloist’s diploma in organ and a teacher’s diploma in piano. Rae Linda Brown, her biographer, writes that she studied composition there with Wallace Goodrich and Frederick Converse and studied privately with the conservatory’s director, George W. Chadwick; the Song of America project likewise records private composition lessons with him.

edges.title: Price’s Symphony No. 1 after Dvořák’s New World

works.from: Dvořák, Symphony No. 9 “From the New World” (1893) and the American works
works.to: Price, Symphony No. 1 in E minor (begun January 1931)

edges.claim: [[price]] began her Symphony in E minor in January 1931 and worked on it for much of the year. It won a Rodman Wanamaker prize in 1932, and Frederick Stock conducted the Chicago Symphony in its first performance on 15 June 1933. Like [[dvorak]]’s “New World” Symphony, it has four movements in the familiar order. Phillip Huscher heard its opening, a syncopated bassoon solo, as at once recalling the “New World”, and Rae Linda Brown found Dvořák’s influence “most evident” in the second theme of the first movement. Brown added that the “American” works Dvořák wrote while heading the National Conservatory in New York inspired a generation of American composers, Black and white.

edges.title: Spiritual theme in Price’s Fantasie nègre

works.from: “Sinner, Please Don’t Let This Harvest Pass”, African American spiritual
works.to: Price, Fantasie nègre (1929), dedicated to Margaret Bonds

edges.claim: In 1929 [[price]] dedicated her Fantasie nègre to the young Margaret Bonds. Samantha Ege writes that Price took her theme from the spiritual “Sinner, Please Don’t Let This Harvest Pass”. The pianist Lara Downes recalls it as the first post-Romantic virtuoso piece she had heard that was built on a spiritual melody, and found that it moved audiences wherever she played it. A dance troupe led by Ludmilla Speranza and Katherine Dunham later staged the work as a ballet, with Bonds at the piano.

edges.title: Anderson singing Price, Lincoln Memorial, 1939

works.from: Marian Anderson’s concert at the Lincoln Memorial, Washington, 9 April 1939
works.to: Price’s arrangement of “My Soul’s Been Anchored in de Lord”

edges.claim: When the Daughters of the American Revolution refused [[marian-anderson]] the use of Constitution Hall because she was Black, an open-air concert was arranged on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial. On Easter Sunday, 9 April 1939, she sang to a crowd of 75,000, with six microphones carrying the concert to radio and Kosti Vehanen at the piano. After “America”, Donizetti’s “O mio Fernando” and Schubert’s “Ave Maria”, she sang three spirituals: Harry T. Burleigh’s arrangement of “Gospel Train”, Edward Boatner’s “Trampin’” and Florence Price’s arrangement of “My Soul’s Been Anchored in the Lord”. According to Rae Linda Brown, Price wrote many of her art songs and spiritual arrangements for Anderson.

edges.title: Florence Price and Margaret Bonds in Chicago

works.from: Price as teacher and mentor in the Bonds household, Chicago
works.to: Bonds’s song prize in the 1932 Wanamaker competition; Price’s Fantasie nègre (1929), dedicated to her

edges.claim: When [[price]] moved to Chicago in 1927 she was welcomed into the Bonds family. After her marriage ended, the pianist Estella Bonds, whom she had met through the city’s Black music organisations, invited Price and her daughters to live in her three-storey house. Price taught and mentored Estella’s daughter Margaret and dedicated her Fantasie nègre to her. Bonds went on to play Price’s works often. In 1932 Price’s symphony and piano sonata won Rodman Wanamaker prizes, and Bonds won one for a song. According to Arionne Nettles, Bonds, under Price’s tutelage, went on to become one of the great composers of the Chicago Black Renaissance.

edges.title: Copland’s studies with Nadia Boulanger, 1921–24

works.from: Boulanger’s harmony and composition classes, Fontainebleau and Paris, 1921–24
works.to: Copland, Symphony for Organ and Orchestra (first played 1925)

edges.claim: In May 1921 [[copland]] enrolled at the newly established American Conservatory at Fontainebleau. A friend urged him to attend the harmony class of a young Frenchwoman, Nadia Boulanger. He later remembered hesitating, “because I had never heard of any composer who had studied with a woman”, but he chose her as his teacher and began composition studies with her in October. A year of study in France became three. In 1924 Boulanger took him to meet Koussevitzky in Paris; after hearing part of Copland’s ballet Grohg at the piano, the conductor ordered an organ concerto for Boulanger to play. It became the Symphony for Organ and Orchestra, which she played in New York in 1925 under Walter Damrosch. Copland often said, “I don’t know what my career would have been like without her!”

edges.title: Copland’s mentoring of Bernstein, 1937

works.from: Copland’s Piano Variations (1930) and his letters to Bernstein from 1937
works.to: Bernstein’s arrangements of El Salón México; the Third Symphony performances of the 1940s

edges.claim: On 14 November 1937 the Harvard undergraduate Leonard Bernstein sat next to [[copland]] at a dance recital in New York, and the poet Muriel Rukeyser introduced them. Bernstein had already studied and performed Copland’s Piano Variations. Copland invited him to his birthday party that night and began a correspondence in which he wrote as counsellor and addressed him as “Dear Pupil”. Bernstein often called Copland the closest he came to having a real composition teacher. The first published works under his name were the solo and two-piano arrangements of El Salón México that Copland asked him to make. In the 1940s he conducted many of the early performances of the Third Symphony and cut a few bars from its finale on his own initiative. Copland came to agree with the cut, and according to Vivian Perlis it was the only such change he ever accepted.

sources.title: Michael Boriskin: “Aaron Copland at 125: A Defining Musical Friendship”, Leonard Bernstein Office (18 November 2025)

edges.title: Chávez and Copland in Mexico, 1932

works.from: Chávez’s invitation and the first all-Copland concert, Mexico City, 2 September 1932
works.to: Copland, El Salón México (1932–36), conducted by Chávez at the première, 27 August 1937

edges.claim: [[carlos-chavez]] arranged Copland’s first visit to Mexico in 1932 and organised the first all-Copland programme, at the Conservatorio Nacional on 2 September: the Two Pieces for String Quartet, the Piano Variations, the Two Pieces for Chorus and Music for the Theatre. He also took his friend to a nightclub called El Salón México. “I was attracted by the spirit of the place and by the Mexican people,” Copland said. “Using Mexican melodies seemed appropriate.” He finished the orchestral piece in 1936, and Chávez conducted the Orquesta Sinfónica de México in the first performance, in Mexico City on 27 August 1937.

edges.title: Stepp’s Bonaparte’s Retreat in Copland’s Hoe-Down

works.from: W. H. Stepp, “Bonaparte’s Retreat”, recorded by Alan and Elizabeth Lomax, Salyersville, Kentucky, October 1937

edges.claim: In October 1937 Alan and Elizabeth Lomax recorded the Kentucky fiddler [[william-hamilton-stepp]] at Salyersville playing “Bonaparte’s Retreat”. Stepp nearly doubled the tempo of the old march tune, turning a 4/4 march into a reel or hoedown. When Agnes de Mille asked [[copland]] in April 1942 to score Rodeo, he worked from Ruth Crawford Seeger’s transcription of Stepp’s version in the Lomaxes’ book Our Singing Country (1941), and adopted it nearly note for note, Alan Jabbour writes, as the main theme of the final “Hoe-Down”. He added the fiddle tunes “Hop Light Ladies” and “Gilderoy”. The Library of Congress’s account is that Copland probably never heard the field recording. The Ballet Russe de Monte Carlo gave Rodeo its first performance in New York on 16 October 1942.

edges.title: Gershwin’s studies with Hambitzer, 1913–18

works.from: Charles Hambitzer’s piano lessons, from about early 1913 until 1918
works.to: Gershwin’s earliest songs; his work as a song plugger for Remick from May 1914

edges.claim: [[gershwin|George Gershwin]]’s first important piano teacher was Charles Hambitzer, whom he later described as “the first great musical influence in my life”. The Library of Congress dates the lessons from about early 1913 until Hambitzer’s death in 1918, though it is uncertain how often they met in the later years. From 1912 Gershwin had attended concerts by Leopold Godowsky, Josef Lhévinne, Leo Ornstein and Efrem Zimbalist. In May 1914, at fifteen, by then a skilled sight-reader and transposer, he left school to work as a piano pounder at Jerome H. Remick and Company.

edges.title: Gershwin’s Porgy and Bess after Heyward’s Porgy

works.from: DuBose Heyward’s novel Porgy and the play he and Dorothy Heyward adapted from it
works.to: Gershwin, Porgy and Bess, Alvin Theatre, New York, 10 October 1935

edges.claim: In October 1926 [[gershwin|George Gershwin]] read DuBose Heyward’s novel Porgy and saw its operatic possibilities. He mentioned the idea to Heyward soon afterwards, but serious work began only in November 1933, when Heyward sent him the draft libretto for the first scenes, with more to follow early in 1934. The opera was credited to the Gershwins and the Heywards and based on the novel and on the play Heyward and his wife Dorothy adapted from it. It took about twenty months, eleven of them for composition and nine for orchestration. It opened at Boston’s Colonial Theatre on 30 September 1935 and at the Alvin Theatre in New York on 10 October, with Todd Duncan and Anne Wiggins Brown in the title roles, and ran for 124 performances.

edges.title: Cage’s studies with Schoenberg, Los Angeles, 1935

works.from: Schoenberg’s analysis, counterpoint and composition classes, Los Angeles, from 18 March 1935
works.to: Cage’s rhythmic structures at the Cornish School, Seattle, late 1930s

edges.claim: After preparation with Henry Cowell and Adolph Weiss, [[cage|John Cage]] asked [[schoenberg]] to teach him. Schoenberg warned that he probably could not afford his price; Cage said he had no money, and when he answered yes to the question whether he would devote his life to music, Schoenberg taught him free of charge. From 18 March 1935 Cage studied analysis in small group sessions at Schoenberg’s Hollywood home, and he also attended a private counterpoint class and classes in composition, harmony and counterpoint at the University of Southern California and then at UCLA. After two years it was clear to both of them, Cage remembered, that he had no feeling for harmony, which for Schoenberg was structural. “You’ll come to a wall and won’t be able to get through,” Schoenberg told him. “Then I’ll spend my life knocking my head against that wall,” Cage answered. At the Cornish School in Seattle he made what he called his response to Schoenberg’s structural harmony: a rhythmic structure in which the large parts of a piece have the same proportion as the phrases of a single unit.

edges.title: Cage’s Satie festival, Black Mountain, 1948

works.from: Satie’s music and his play Le Piège de Méduse (1913)
works.to: Cage’s Satie festival and Defense of Satie, Black Mountain College, summer 1948; the Vexations performance, 1963

edges.claim: [[cage|John Cage]] came to know the music of [[satie]] in Paris in 1930, and it remained a source of inspiration for the rest of his life. Teaching at Black Mountain College in July and August 1948, he found that its largely German community did not know Satie’s music, and he organised a festival of twenty-five concerts, each with a short introduction of his own. In the middle of the festival he gave a lecture, Defense of Satie, which set Satie against Beethoven and judged Satie to be right; it caused a controversy. The festival included Satie’s play Le Piège de Méduse, with Buckminster Fuller as Baron Méduse and Elaine de Kooning as Frisette, and Merce Cunningham danced the “Monkey Dances” as Jonas to Cage’s prepared piano. In 1949 Cage published Satie’s Vexations, found in Henri Sauguet’s private collection, in Contrepoints (Paris, no. 6). On 9–10 September 1963 he initiated the first complete performance, at the Pocket Theatre in New York, which lasted eighteen hours and forty minutes and was played by a relay of ten pianists.

sources.locator: Notes on El amor brujo: the Pantomima’s 7/8 metre; Poulenc’s third Novelette in 1959
